questions.stem: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in which Part of the Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: DPSP = Part IV (Articles 36-51), borrowed from the IRISH CONSTITUTION (which borrowed from Spain). Part III = Fundamental Rights (justiciable, enforceable). Part IV-A = Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment 1976, non-justiciable). DPSPs are NON-JUSTICIABLE — cannot be enforced by courts — but 'FUNDAMENTAL IN THE GOVERNANCE OF THE COUNTRY' (Article 37). Aim: build a WELFARE STATE. Classification into 3 groups by the nature of principles: (1) SOCIALIST — aimed at economic + social democracy (Arts 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 47); (2) GANDHIAN — based on Gandhi's ideals (Arts 40, 43, 46, 47, 48); (3) LIBERAL-INTELLECTUAL — liberal democratic ideals (Arts 44, 45, 48, 49, 50, 51). DPSP + FR + FD together = Conscience of the Constitution (Granville Austin).

questions.stem: Article 44 of the DPSP directs the State to endeavour to secure:

options.option_text: UNIFORM CIVIL CODE for all citizens throughout India
Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs (Art 47)

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 44 — directs the State to endeavour to secure a UNIFORM CIVIL CODE (UCC) for all citizens throughout India. A UCC would replace personal laws (based on religion — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi, etc.) with a common set of laws governing every citizen — on matters of marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption, etc. Currently only GOA has a UCC (Portuguese legacy). UTTARAKHAND became the first state to enact a UCC bill in Feb 2024 (now law). Controversial — seen by supporters as essential for equality, secularism; by opponents as threat to religious/cultural diversity. LANDMARK CASES: Shah Bano (1985 — SC ruled Muslim woman entitled to alimony under CrPC 125, Parliament overturned via Muslim Women Act 1986); Sarla Mudgal (1995); Shayara Bano (2017 — triple talaq unconstitutional). Other famous DPSPs: ART 40 — Village Panchayats (implemented via 73rd Amendment 1992); ART 45 — early childhood care + free compulsory education for all under 14 (became FR via 86th Amendment 2002 → Art 21-A); ART 50 — separation of judiciary from executive.

questions.stem: The concept of DPSP was borrowed from the Constitution of:
questions.explanation: DPSP was borrowed from the IRISH CONSTITUTION of 1937 (Ireland itself borrowed from the Spanish Constitution of 1931). Major sources of different Indian constitutional provisions: (1) IRELAND: DPSP, method of election of President, nomination of RS members. (2) UK: Parliamentary government, single citizenship, PM + CoM, bicameralism, rule of law, writs. (3) USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment of Judges + President, VP role, SC (original + appellate jurisdiction). (4) CANADA: Federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, appointment of Governors by Centre, advisory SC jurisdiction. (5) AUSTRALIA: Concurrent List, trade + commerce provisions, Joint Sitting of Parliament. (6) USSR: Fundamental Duties, Five-Year Plans, Ideals of Justice (social/economic/political) in Preamble. (7) FRANCE: 'Republic' + Liberty/Equality/Fraternity in Preamble. (8) SOUTH AFRICA: Amendment procedure, RS elections by proportional representation. (9) GERMANY (WEIMAR): Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency. (10) JAPAN: 'Procedure established by law' phrase (Art 21).

Only after Parliament passes enabling legislation

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 37 — DPSPs are NOT enforceable by any court. Cannot be enforced by a court of law in case of violation. However, they are 'FUNDAMENTAL IN THE GOVERNANCE OF THE COUNTRY' and 'IT SHALL BE THE DUTY OF THE STATE TO APPLY THESE PRINCIPLES in making laws'. In short, DPSPs are MORAL MANDATES, not legal obligations. Philosophy: DPSP = positive direction to State; FR = negative restriction on State. DPSP harmonisation with FR: (1) SHANKARI PRASAD v UNION (1951) — DPSP cannot override FR. (2) CHAMPAKAM DORAIRAJAN (1951) — FR prevails over DPSP (led to 1st Amendment). (3) GOLAKNATH (1967) — FR untouchable even via amendment. (4) KESAVANANDA BHARATI (1973) — Basic Structure doctrine; certain FR + DPSP both part of basic structure. (5) MINERVA MILLS (1980) — 'HARMONIOUS CONSTRUCTION' between FR + DPSP; both are equally important. Parliament tried to give DPSP supremacy (42nd Amendment, Arts 31-C), largely struck down in Minerva Mills. Today: DPSP guides policy; FR guarantees rights.

questions.stem: Which article of the DPSP deals with 'PROMOTION OF INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY'?
questions.explanation: ARTICLE 51 — directs the State to endeavour to: (a) promote INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY; (b) maintain JUST AND HONOURABLE RELATIONS between nations; (c) foster respect for INTERNATIONAL LAW + treaty obligations; (d) encourage settlement of INTERNATIONAL DISPUTES BY ARBITRATION. This reflects Nehru's vision of Panchsheel + Non-Aligned Movement. India has been an active UN member, UNPKF contributor, G20 presidency 2023, etc. IMPORTANT DPSPs by Article number: Art 38 — welfare state; Art 39 — equitable distribution of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protection of children; Art 39-A (added 42nd) — free legal aid; Art 40 — organise village panchayats; Art 41 — right to work, education, public assistance; Art 42 — just + humane working conditions + maternity relief; Art 43 — living wages; Art 43-A (42nd) — workers' participation in management; Art 43-B (97th, 2011) — co-operative societies; Art 44 — UCC; Art 45 — early childhood education (originally up to 14, now with Art 21-A); Art 46 — promote SC/ST/BC interests; Art 47 — prohibition of liquor, narcotic drugs; Art 48 — agriculture + husbandry + cow protection; Art 48-A (42nd) — protect environment; Art 49 — protect monuments; Art 50 — separate judiciary from executive; Art 51 — international peace.

questions.stem: Article 47 of DPSP directs the State to raise the level of nutrition + standard of living and specifically to:

options.option_text: Bring about PROHIBITION of consumption of INTOXICATING DRINKS and DRUGS injurious to health

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 47 — 'The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition + the standard of living + the improvement of public health as among its primary duties and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about PROHIBITION of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of INTOXICATING DRINKS AND DRUGS which are injurious to health.' GANDHIAN principle. Implementation: Some Indian STATES have imposed prohibition (wholly or partly) — GUJARAT (since 1960), BIHAR (since 2016 under Nitish Kumar), MIZORAM, NAGALAND, LAKSHADWEEP. Most states follow partial regulations (dry days, age limits). Kerala had a brief prohibition attempt (2014-17, rolled back). Other Gandhian DPSPs: Art 40 (Panchayati Raj), Art 43 (cottage industries), Art 46 (SC/ST/weaker section welfare), Art 48 (COW PROTECTION ban on cow slaughter — implemented via state laws; cow slaughter banned in many states but varies), Art 43-B (cooperatives). The Constitution's Gandhian flavor — especially Parts III and IV — reflects the values central to India's freedom struggle.

questions.stem: Article 39(b) + 39(c) of DPSP — directing equitable distribution of material resources for the common good — were given PRIMACY over certain FRs by the 25th Amendment (1971) via:
questions.explanation: ARTICLE 31-C — inserted by 25th AMENDMENT (1971) under Indira Gandhi. Originally said: any law enacted to give effect to the DPSPs contained in Articles 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be challenged on grounds of violating Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms), 31 (property). The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended this protection to ALL DPSPs (not just 39b/c). MINERVA MILLS v UNION (1980) — SC STRUCK DOWN the 42nd Amendment's extension (saying it violated the Basic Structure by making DPSP supreme over FR without balance). So TODAY, Art 31-C's original scope — protection ONLY for laws under Art 39(b) and 39(c) — survives. 39(b) — 'ownership and control of material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good'; 39(c) — 'operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment'. These were the key enabling provisions for NATIONALISATION drives + LAND REFORMS. LIC nationalisation (1956), Bank nationalisation (1969, 1980), Coal nationalisation (1973) — all grounded in Art 39.
